description.summary: Weaviate is an open-source dedicated vector database that combines vector similarity search, structured pre-filtering, BM25F keyword retrieval, and configurable hybrid fusion.
description.description: Weaviate stores objects and vectors and supports HNSW, flat, dynamic, and disk-oriented HFresh vector indexes. It combines vector retrieval with inverted-index filtering and BM25F keyword search, provides named and multi-vector retrieval, supports multi-tenancy, sharding, replication, tunable consistency, and several vector quantization methods, and can run self-hosted or through Weaviate Cloud. This record separates documented engine capabilities from workload-, configuration-, and deployment-dependent behavior.

indexingConsiderations: Choose HNSW for high query throughput, flat for small isolated indexes, dynamic for one-way flat-to-HNSW growth, or HFresh when reducing memory use is more important than peak query throughput.
Configure inverted and range indexes only for properties used by filtering, BM25F, sorting, or aggregation because each additional index consumes storage and ingestion resources.
Benchmark rotational, product, scalar, or binary quantization with the actual embeddings because compression changes recall, memory, storage, and rescoring cost.
Plan shard count, replication factor, tenant count, and replica movement for the expected cluster topology before large-scale ingestion.
retrievalConsiderations: Evaluate vector-only, BM25F-only, and hybrid retrieval on the same relevance set before selecting alpha and the fusion strategy.
Use indexed pre-filters and test selective filters with the chosen HNSW, flat, dynamic, or HFresh configuration.
Treat named and multi-vector spaces as separate retrieval representations with explicit target vectors, metrics, and evaluation criteria.
Select read and write consistency levels according to the required tradeoff among availability, latency, and replica convergence.

limitations: HNSW, flat, dynamic, and HFresh indexes have different tradeoffs among import cost, memory, disk I/O, recall, latency, and query throughput.
The dynamic index requires asynchronous indexing and performs a one-way transition from flat to HNSW rather than switching back after the object count falls.
HFresh keeps most vector data on disk and targets memory efficiency rather than maximum HNSW-like query throughput; it also supports only cosine and squared-L2 distance.
Vector quantization is lossy and requires workload-specific rescoring and recall evaluation.
Read consistency controls retrieval of identified objects but does not merge search-result UUID lists from every replica.
Replication, shard movement, backup behavior, encryption, and operational automation depend on the chosen self-hosted or managed deployment.
Weaviate does not provide general multi-record ACID transactions comparable to a relational database.
usageGuidance: Record the Weaviate server and client versions because index, replication, module, and query behavior evolves across releases.
Use a representative relevance and load test before changing index type, filter strategy, fusion, quantization, or consistency settings.
Use multi-tenancy when tenant isolation and per-tenant lifecycle management are required, while accounting for one shard per tenant.
Test backup and restoration procedures and replica-repair behavior instead of treating replication as a backup substitute.
Monitor memory, disk, indexing queues, shard distribution, query latency, recall, and replica consistency in production.

references.title: Weaviate v1.38.5: LSM store performance improvements, batch vectorization deadlock fixes, and allocation-free reference cache improvements

claims.statement: Weaviate supports HNSW, flat, dynamic, and HFresh vector indexes and documents cosine, dot-product, squared-L2, Hamming, and Manhattan distance options, subject to index-specific constraints.
claims.rationale: The official vector-index reference lists four index types, while the distance reference enumerates the supported metrics and notes that HFresh supports only cosine and squared L2.

claims.statement: Weaviate performs structured pre-filtering by building an inverted-index allow-list before vector search and applying it during vector-index traversal.

qualifiers.name: configurationScope
qualifiers.value: Relevant properties must have appropriate inverted or range indexes

claims.rationale: The official filtering documentation explicitly describes pre-filtering through an inverted-index allow-list passed to the vector index.

claims.statement: Weaviate hybrid search combines vector retrieval with BM25F keyword retrieval and supports configurable weighting plus relative-score or rank-based fusion.

qualifiers.name: versionScope
qualifiers.value: Relative-score fusion is the documented default from Weaviate 1.24 onward

claims.rationale: The official hybrid-search documentation defines the parallel vector and BM25F legs, alpha weighting, relative-score fusion, and ranked fusion.

claims.statement: Weaviate supports sharding and replicated multi-node collections; cluster metadata uses Raft, while data objects use leaderless replication with tunable read and write consistency.

qualifiers.name: consistencyScope
qualifiers.value: Object-level read consistency does not merge query-result identifier lists from every replica

claims.rationale: The replication documentation distinguishes Raft-replicated cluster metadata from leaderless object replication and documents ONE, QUORUM, and ALL consistency levels; multi-tenancy stores each tenant on a separate shard.

claims.statement: Weaviate supports rotational, product, scalar, and binary vector quantization, and its HFresh index keeps most vector data on disk while retaining a compressed centroid index in memory.

qualifiers.name: performanceScope
qualifiers.value: Compression and HFresh require workload-specific recall, latency, memory, and I/O evaluation

claims.rationale: The official compression documentation lists four quantization families, and the vector-index documentation describes the disk-oriented HFresh architecture and its mandatory rotational quantization.

evidence.summary: Official Weaviate sources list HNSW, flat, dynamic, and HFresh indexes and enumerate five configurable distance metrics.
evidence.interpretation: The RKM profile can model exact flat search, HNSW, a disk-oriented ANN option, and other dynamic index behavior while retaining index-specific metric constraints.

sourceFragments.locator: Vector index sections: supported index types, HNSW, flat, dynamic, and HFresh
Available distance metrics and HFresh metric restrictions

limitations: Project documentation establishes supported behavior but is not an independent benchmark.
Index performance depends on collection size, vector distribution, hardware, filters, compression, and tuning.

evidence.summary: The Weaviate filtering documentation describes pre-filtering with an inverted-index allow-list supplied to vector search.
evidence.interpretation: Weaviate supports filtered retrieval without relying on a post-filter-only candidate pipeline, provided the required scalar indexes exist.

sourceFragments.locator: Filtering sections: pre-filtering, inverted-index allow-lists, ACORN strategy, and flat-search cutoff

limitations: Indexing additional properties consumes storage and ingestion resources.
Highly selective filters can trigger different search paths, so latency and recall still require workload testing.

evidence.summary: The hybrid-search documentation combines vector and BM25F retrieval and documents alpha weighting, relative-score fusion, and ranked fusion.
evidence.interpretation: The RKM profile can mark built-in BM25-plus-vector retrieval, weighted fusion, and score normalization.

sourceFragments.locator: Hybrid search sections: vector and BM25F legs, alpha, Relative Score Fusion, and Ranked Fusion

limitations: No alpha or fusion method is universally optimal across datasets and relevance objectives.
Score normalization can make results sensitive to candidate set composition and query limits.

evidence.summary: Weaviate documents Raft for cluster metadata, leaderless object replication, tunable ONE, QUORUM, and ALL consistency, and per-tenant shards.
evidence.interpretation: The RKM profile can mark high horizontal scaling, sharding, replication, multi-tenancy, and configurable consistency while retaining query-consistency caveats.

sourceFragments.locator: Consistency sections: Raft metadata, leaderless data objects, read/write consistency, and query caveat
Multi-tenancy sections: tenant isolation, separate shards, and tenant lifecycle states

limitations: Consistency levels change acknowledgment and object-retrieval behavior but do not make every search-result list globally merged across replicas.
Tenant and replica counts affect memory, shard management, and operational complexity.

evidence.summary: Weaviate documents RQ, PQ, SQ, and BQ compression and describes HFresh as a disk-oriented index with compressed in-memory centroids.
evidence.interpretation: The RKM profile can include product and scalar quantization, other compression families, and disk-backed ANN while preserving lossy compression and I/O tradeoffs.

sourceFragments.locator: HFresh sections: centroid HNSW, disk posting lists, mandatory RQ, and tuning parameters
Vector quantization sections: RQ, PQ, SQ, BQ, rescoring, and index compatibility

limitations: Quantization is lossy, and rescoring or over-fetching can add latency and I/O.
HFresh prioritizes memory efficiency and predictable disk I/O rather than peak HNSW query throughput.
